blocks.text: Microbiological pollution is the contamination of water by harmful microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, protozoa and parasites, which can seriously harm humans and animals. It usually comes from untreated or poorly treated sewage, animal waste, hospital waste and runoff from farmland. Common pathogens in such water include Escherichia coli, Salmonella and Giardia. Microorganisms in water are the major cause of water-borne diseases such as cholera, typhoid, dysentery and hepatitis A. Boiling water (100 C) kills most bacteria, viruses and protozoa and makes water drinkable, but boiling alone cannot remove other pollutants.

blocks.text: Chemical pollution often includes toxic heavy metals such as mercury, lead, arsenic and cadmium, and farm chemicals such as pesticides and herbicides. Heavy metals enter water through industrial discharge, mining and improper waste disposal.

items: Mercury enters water mainly from coal burning, gold mining, and industrial waste from thermometer or battery manufacture. In sediments, bacteria convert inorganic mercury into methylmercury ([CH3Hg]+), which is more dangerous.
The major sources of lead are leaded petrol (now banned worldwide), old plumbing (lead pipes), lead-acid batteries and paints. Lead ions (Pb2+) often enter water through the corrosion of pipes.
Metal plating, plastic stabilisers and impurities in phosphate fertilisers are major sources of cadmium in water.

blocks.text: Heavy metals have high atomic masses and densities. Because they are not biodegradable, they tend to accumulate in the tissues of living organisms and are particularly dangerous. Methylmercury is highly fat-soluble, so it easily crosses biological membranes and undergoes biomagnification; it is a potent neurotoxin that crosses the blood-brain barrier, and long exposure leads to Minamata disease (ataxia, numbness in the hands and feet, and general muscle weakness). Lead interferes with the production of haemoglobin, leading to anaemia; in children it is a cumulative poison that causes irreversible neurological damage and developmental delays. Long-term intake of cadmium leads to itai-itai disease, in which cadmium replaces calcium in the bones and makes them extremely brittle; it also causes severe kidney damage (nephrotoxicity).

blocks.caption: Cd2+ ions have higher charge density so they can replace Ca2+ ions in bones (original drawing after the textbook's illustration).

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: The Minamata disaster was a severe case of industrial pollution in the 1950s in Minamata, Japan. Methylmercury released into the water caused widespread mercury poisoning, affecting thousands of people with neurological damage and causing birth defects, deaths and environmental devastation.

Pesticides and herbicides such as DDT and glyphosate are another hazardous group that pollutes water and causes severe health problems. Their major sources are agricultural runoff and domestic gardening. Many are non-polar and insoluble in water but very soluble in the fatty tissues of fish and birds. Many older pesticides such as DDT are persistent organic pollutants (POPs). Pesticides are linked to hormonal disruption and developmental problems, and chemical pollution also degrades water quality, reduces biodiversity and disrupts aquatic ecosystems.

Many pesticides act as endocrine disruptors that mimic natural hormones such as oestrogen. This can lead to reproductive failure in wildlife (for example thinning of eggshells in birds) and is linked to hormonal cancers in humans. Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) were used as coolants in electrical transformers; they leak into water from hazardous waste sites, are classified as probable human carcinogens, suppress the immune system and cause skin conditions such as chloracne.

blocks.text: Nutrient pollution, also called eutrophication, occurs when excessive amounts of nutrients, mainly nitrogen and phosphorus, enter water bodies, usually from agricultural runoff, wastewater discharge and stormwater. Although these nutrients are essential for plant growth, their excess leads to the rapid growth of algae (algal blooms). The blooms can block sunlight from underwater plants. When the algae die and decompose they use up large amounts of oxygen, creating hypoxic 'dead zones' where aquatic life cannot survive. Eutrophication disrupts aquatic ecosystems, reduces biodiversity, harms fisheries and spoils water for drinking and recreation. High nitrate levels in drinking water are particularly dangerous for infants and can cause 'blue baby syndrome' (methaemoglobinaemia), in which nitrates reduce the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.

Oil pollution in the oceans, particularly from leaks and spills from ships, is a major environmental threat. Spilled oil spreads rapidly across the water surface as a layer that blocks sunlight and reduces oxygen exchange. This severely harms marine life, including fish, birds and mammals; marine mammals can swallow the toxic oil while grooming, and fish may suffer long-term harm from hydrocarbons. Oil pollution also damages coastal habitats such as mangroves, coral reefs and beaches.

Plastic and solid-waste pollution in oceans and other water bodies is a growing environmental crisis. Millions of tonnes of plastic waste, including bottles, bags, fishing nets and microplastics, are dumped into rivers, lakes and oceans every year. Unlike organic materials, plastics do not biodegrade; they break into smaller particles that persist for centuries. Marine animals often mistake plastic for food, leading to swallowing, choking or internal injury, which can be fatal, and entanglement in old fishing gear and other debris injures or kills countless turtles, dolphins and birds. Microplastics have entered the food chain, raising concerns about their effects on human health. Solid waste also clogs waterways, disrupts aquatic habitats and lowers water quality.
